content.p: Lyle and Erik Menendez were convicted in 1996 of murdering their parents, José and Kitty Menendez, in the family's Beverly Hills mansion in August 1989. They were 21 and 18 at the time. Two earlier trials, with a separate jury for each brother, had ended in deadlock. At a second trial, a single jury found both guilty of first-degree murder, and each was sentenced to life without the possibility of parole.

The brothers admitted the shootings. They said they had killed after years of abuse by their father and out of fear for their lives, while prosecutors said the motive was money. For nearly three decades the sentence did not move. Then a Netflix drama and a Peacock documentary revived public interest, a new district attorney's review followed, and in May 2025 a judge cut the sentences to 50 years to life. Parole boards refused release in August 2025. In September 2026 the brothers were granted an earlier parole hearing, tentatively set for March 2027.

According to the Los Angeles Times, José Menendez, 45, and his wife Kitty, 44, were watching television at home on the evening of 20 August when they were shot with 12-gauge shotguns. The newspaper reported that their two sons, Lyle and "Eric" in the paper's spelling, found them after a night out. Police later said José had been shot in the back of the head, and that Kitty, who did not die at once, tried to run and was shot several times. Both also had wounds to a kneecap, according to NBC Los Angeles.
The brothers called 911 at about 11:47 p.m., saying they had come home from the movies and a festival. CNN's timeline quotes Lyle telling the operator: "Someone killed my parents."

In the days after the killings, detectives did not look first at the sons. On 30 August 1989 the Times reported that law enforcement sources believed at least two hit men had carried out a "message killing" in organised-crime style, and that investigators were examining José's business ties. The Beverly Hills police spokesman said the department was "not absolutely convinced it was anything, including organized crime." EBSCO's account says police turned to the sons within weeks, as they gave up plans for college and spent heavily on cars, clothes and jewellery. NBC Los Angeles reports that prosecutors later alleged the brothers spent $1 million in six months.

The case turned on a therapist. According to EBSCO, Erik told his psychologist, Dr. Jerome Oziel, in October 1989 that he and Lyle had killed their parents. Five months later Oziel's girlfriend, Judalon Smyth, contacted police and said Oziel had recorded it. Lyle was arrested on 8 March 1990, and Erik, who had been in Israel, surrendered three days after his return to Los Angeles, NBC Los Angeles reports.

The recordings did not reach a jury quickly. EBSCO says the case stalled on a dispute about therapist-client confidentiality before juries were finally allowed to hear parts of the tapes. Murder charges were filed after a judge ruled the recordings admissible.

The first trial opened in July 1993, was shown live on Court TV, and was heard by two juries, one for each brother. Prosecutors argued the killings were for financial gain. The defence told jurors that the brothers had acted in self-defence after years of emotional, psychological and sexual abuse by José. In January 1994 both juries deadlocked.

The retrial began in October 1995 with one jury for both men. This time much of the defence evidence about abuse was excluded, according to the defence attorneys quoted by CNN. The Hollywood Reporter adds that the brothers' argument was imperfect self-defence, an honest but unreasonable belief that deadly force was necessary, and that the judge ruled the evidence did not support a claim of imminent danger.

On 20 March 1996 the jury convicted both of first-degree murder. The Hollywood Reporter says the verdict included a lying-in-wait element. The brothers were sentenced in July 1996 to life without parole. Each received two such terms, according to ABC News and EBSCO. Their appeals over the following years failed, according to a report carried by KAXE.
content.h2: New evidence and a prosecutor's change of mind
content.p: In May 2023 the Peacock documentary "Menendez + Menudo: Boys Betrayed" aired. In it a former member of the boy band Menudo, Roy Rosselló, said in a sworn statement that José Menendez had raped him when he was about 14. That same month the brothers' lawyers filed a habeas corpus petition asking a court to reconsider the convictions, citing Rosselló's statement and a letter Erik wrote to his cousin Andy Cano before the killings, describing abuse by his father. Rolling Stone, quoting the petition, says Erik wrote the letter eight months before the shootings, when he was 17. "It's still happening Andy but it's worse for me now," the letter reads.

In September 2024 Netflix released "Monsters: The Lyle and Erik Menendez Story," a nine-episode drama. Erik publicly criticised it, saying it contained "horrible and blatant lies." The following month Los Angeles County District Attorney George Gascón told CNN there was no question the brothers had committed the killings, and that the question was "to what degree of culpability" they should be held accountable. He said a jury today would probably view the case very differently than a jury did 35 years earlier. On 24 October 2024 he announced that he would ask the court to resentence them to 50 years to life. "I believe they have paid their debt to society," he said, according to CBS News. Because both were under 26 at the time of the crime, they would then be immediately eligible for parole.
Kitty Menendez's brother, Milton Andersen, objected in a court filing, arguing that the brothers "meticulously planned and executed the cold-blooded murders of both their parents."

Gascón lost his election weeks later. His successor, Nathan Hochman, took office on 3 December 2024 and reviewed the files. On 10 March 2025 he asked the court to withdraw the resentencing motion and called the self-defence claim a series of "lies." He said the brothers had told 20 lies and admitted only four. He pointed to premeditation, saying the brothers bought shotguns with a fake ID, planned an alibi and discarded their clothes. He said that if the brothers ever fully accepted responsibility, his office would take that into account. Lyle posted on Facebook that several of the "lies" had been admitted or stipulated to at the first trial and that others were disputed. A judge denied Hochman's request to withdraw the recommendation.

Governor Gavin Newsom had said in November 2024 that he would wait for the new prosecutor's review before deciding on the brothers' clemency application. On 26 February 2025 he ordered the parole board to carry out a 90-day risk assessment, adding: "There's no guarantee of outcome here." In May 2025 the board's executive officer told lawyers that Newsom had withdrawn that request in light of the resentencing, though the governor's office noted that the clemency application remained active. The risk assessments concluded that the brothers would pose a "moderate" risk of violence if released, according to CNN's account.

At a hearing in Van Nuys, Judge Michael Jesic ruled in May 2025 to cut the sentences to 50 years to life. He said a horrific crime had been committed but that he was equally shocked by letters from prison and corrections officers, calling what the brothers had done "remarkable." He said he was not suggesting they should be released, but that "one day they should get that chance." The decision, he said, was "now up to the parole board and the governor of California."

Both brothers appeared remotely. Erik said: "I committed an atrocious act against two people who had every right to live, my mom and dad." Lyle said he "was immature" and "filled with rage." Hochman said in a statement that the decision was "a monumental one" and said the brothers must admit their claims were fabricated before resentencing could be justified. Their attorney, Mark Geragos, said redemption is possible.

Hearings were set for 21 and 22 August 2025. Erik's lasted nearly ten hours. Commissioner Robert Barton said the primary reason for denial was his conduct in prison rather than the seriousness of the crime. "Contrary to your supporters' beliefs, you have not been a model prisoner," Barton said. Among the violations the panel listed were involvement in a tax-fraud scheme for a prison gang, violent incidents in 1997 and 2011, drug and alcohol use, and having a cellphone. Erik told the panel that since he had no hope of release, he had put protecting himself ahead of rules until November 2024, when "now the consequences mattered." Barton said the way Erik shot his mother showed him to be "devoid of human compassion" at the time. He also told him: "Two things can be true. They can love and forgive you, and you can still be found unsuitable for parole."

Lyle's hearing ran more than 11 hours before a different two-person panel. Commissioner Julie Garland said he had shown genuine remorse and "demonstrated the potential for change" but still posed a risk to the public. A commissioner said his violence was impulsive and showed "poor threat perception" and called the reloading and final shot that killed Kitty "callous." The Guardian reported that the board said Lyle still displayed "anti-social personality traits like deception." Lyle said at the hearing that his mother had also sexually abused him, which, Garland confirmed, had not been included in his risk assessment. The panels heard that both brothers had numerous violations for contraband cellphones; Lyle had pleaded guilty to two, in November 2024 and March 2025.
Each brother was denied for three years, the shortest interval allowed. Hochman welcomed the decisions but said parole could be considered if Lyle accepted full responsibility.

In July 2025 Judge William Ryan ordered prosecutors to show why the 2023 petition should not be granted. Some outlets read that order as a victory for the brothers. In September 2025, in a 16-page ruling, he rejected the petition. He called the Cano letter and Rosselló's declaration neither "particularly strong," saying the letter "only corroborates" trial testimony and that Rosselló's account was "not relevant to the petitioners' state of mind at the time of the murders." Evidence that "slightly corroborates" abuse, he wrote, did not negate premeditation or the lying-in-wait finding. The ruling did not affect the parole process.

The Guardian reported that the parole board granted the brothers' requests for earlier hearings on the Friday before 8 September 2026; ABC7 and Good Morning America reported the grant as coming on Monday. Their next hearing, previously available from August 2028, is tentatively set for March 2027. Fox News and The Orange County Register attribute the change to two provisions in Proposition 9 that allow a hearing to be advanced on a change in circumstances or new information. The Guardian quotes the corrections department's wording and says the department did not immediately explain the decision.

The district attorney's office said its position "remains the same whether it's 2027, 2028 or any year after": if the brothers stop breaking prison rules and admit what it calls their lies, "including their biggest lie, the self-defense defense," they might be released. The brothers' family said in a statement that they had worked for almost 40 years to take responsibility, and noted the hospice program and a "Green Space" project they helped create. Fox News reports that Lyle is 58 and Erik 55, and both are held in San Diego.

Several things stay open. The board must decide in 2027 whether the brothers are suitable; if it recommends parole, California's governor can affirm, reverse or modify the decision, as Newsom did when he refused parole to Sirhan Sirhan in 2022. None of the September 2026 coverage reports a decision on the clemency application.
